```{r}
#Part A

#Question 1A
scores <- c(88, 72, 95, 60, 83, 91)
names(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Carl", "Dina", "Eve", "Felix")
scores

#Question 1B
sort(scores)                        
sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)

#Question 1C
sorted_asc <- sort(scores)
print(sorted_asc)

#Question 1D
subjects   <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

#Question 1E
sort(subjects)

#Question 1F
sort(incomplete)

#Question 2
#Yes, the names stayed correctly attached to their original values because they were sorted together. This is important because if the names did not follow their scores, we might identify the wrong student as the top performer.

#Question 3
#This can be dangerous because sort() removes missing values (NA) by default. If we do not check for missing data first, we might report an incorrect lowest score because we would not know that some scores were missing.

#Question 4
order(scores)
sort(scores)

#Question 5  
name    <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")
score   <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
section <- c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")

students <- data.frame(name, score, section)
students

#Question 5A
students[order(students$score), ]

#Question 5B
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]

#Question 6
#order(scores) returns the position or index numbers of the scores arranged from lowest to highest. These numbers are not the actual scores, so they are not very useful on their own. We use them to index the original vector so that the scores will appear in the correct sorted order.

#Question 7
#sort() alone cannot reorder the entire students data frame because it only sorts values instead of keeping the rows and their related information together. The order() function is the correct tool because it arranges the rows based on the scores while keeping each student's name, score, and section properly matched.

#Question 8 (Coding)
scores <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
names(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")

cbind(scores, rank(scores))

#Question 8A
#Both Ben and Dex received rank 6.5.

#Question 8B
#Ben and Dex both scored 92, which are the 6th and 7th highest values when sorted ascending. By default, R’s rank() uses average ranking for ties.

#Question 8A Dataframe
sales <- data.frame(
  employee   = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)

sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)

sales

#Question 8B Dataframe
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]

#Question 9
#No, order() alone cannot solve the entire problem because it only tells us the arrangement of the values, not the actual rank of each student. The rank() function gives each student their standing based on their score, while order() arranges the students from highest to lowest or lowest to highest. We need both functions to know each student's rank and display the table in the correct order.
